title: Writing Through Time: From Clay Tablets to Keyboards
summary: How writing developed from clay tablets in Mesopotamia through picture signs, alphabets, paper, and the printing press to today's keyboards.
poll: The printing press changed the world more than the computer has.

versions.title: From Clay to Keys
versions.text:
Long ago, no one could write. Facts had to stay in your head. If you lost a fact, it was gone.

Then things changed. It was in the land we now call Iraq. Folks there took soft, wet clay. They made flat clay tablets. They took a sharp stick. They pressed marks in the clay. Each mark was a symbol. The marks kept track of grain and sheep.

In Egypt, folks drew small signs. Some looked like birds. Some looked like eyes. They wrote on thin sheets made from a plant.

Next, some folks made an alphabet. Each sign stood for one sound. With a few signs, you could write all your words. Our ABCs came from old sets like this. So did Arabic letters.

Then came paper. It was first made in China. It was light. It did not cost much. It went to Baghdad. Then it went all through the world.

Next came a big press. It could print lots of books fast. Books cost less. Now more folks could read.

Now we tap keys on a keyboard. We send words to the whole world in a flash.

People in Egypt wrote, too. They drew small signs. Some looked like birds, eyes, and hands. They wrote on thin sheets made from a plant.

Then paper was made in China. It was light. It did not cost much. Paper went to Baghdad. Then it spread far and wide.

About 600 years ago, a man in Germany made a big press. It could print lots of books fast. Books cost less. So more people learned to read.

Now we type on a keyboard. We can send words all over the world in a flash.

About 600 years ago, a man in Germany built a printing press. It could print many books fast. Books cost less, so more people learned to read.

Today, many people write by typing on a keyboard. We can send our words around the world in a few seconds.

versions.title: Writing Through Time
versions.text:
Long ago, before people could write, they had to remember everything. They passed on stories, rules, and facts by talking. If someone forgot a fact, it could be lost for good.

About 5,000 years ago, people in Mesopotamia found a new way to save facts. Today, we call that land Iraq. They pressed soft, wet clay into flat tablets. Then they used a sharp reed to push small, wedge-shaped marks into the clay. Each mark was a symbol. At first, these marks were used to count grain, animals, and goods for trade.

In Egypt, people wrote with small signs. The signs looked like birds, eyes, and hands. They often wrote on sheets made from papyrus. It was a tall plant that grew along the Nile River.

Later, people made an alphabet. In an alphabet, each letter stands for a sound. That means a small set of letters can spell any word. Our ABCs and the Arabic letters both grew from old alphabets like this.

Paper was first made in China. It was light and cheap. It was easy to carry, too. Over hundreds of years, paper making spread to Baghdad. From there it reached many other lands.

About 600 years ago, a man in Germany built a printing press. It could print many copies of a book in a short time. Books cost less, so more people learned to read.

Today, many people write by typing on a keyboard. With computers and phones, we can send our words around the world in seconds.

versions.title: Writing Through Time: From Clay Tablets to Keyboards
versions.text:
Before writing, people had to remember everything. Stories, laws, and family histories were passed from one person to the next by speaking. If someone forgot a detail, it could be lost forever. Writing changed that, because it let words last much longer than a voice.

About 5,000 years ago, the Sumerians of Mesopotamia found a way to record facts. Their land is now part of Iraq. They pressed damp clay into flat tablets. Then they used a sharp reed to make small marks shaped like wedges. This kind of writing is called cuneiform, which means "wedge-shaped." At first, it was used to keep track of grain, animals, and trade. Writers called scribes went to school for years to learn hundreds of signs.

In Egypt, scribes wrote with picture signs called hieroglyphs. They often wrote on papyrus. It was a kind of paper made from a tall reed that grew along the Nile River.

About 3,000 years ago, a group of traders called the Phoenicians used an alphabet. An alphabet is a small set of letters that stand for sounds. It was much easier to learn than hundreds of signs, so it spread from place to place. Many later alphabets grew from it, such as the ones used for Arabic and English.

Paper was first made in China about 1,900 years ago. By about the year 800, Baghdad had paper mills. Soon, books and libraries spread across the Islamic world and beyond.

Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg of Germany built a printing press. It had metal letters that could be moved and used again and again. This invention made books faster and cheaper to make, so more people could own them.

The typewriter came in the 1870s. Its keyboard layout is still used today. Now, with computers and phones, we can share our writing around the world in seconds.

versions.title: Writing Through Time: From Clay Tablets to Keyboards
versions.text:
Before writing existed, every civilization had to depend on human memory. Stories, laws, and family histories were passed from one generation to the next through speech. Whenever someone forgot an important detail, that knowledge could vanish forever. Writing transformed this situation, because it allowed words to survive far longer than any human voice.

About 5,000 years ago, the Sumerians of Mesopotamia, in present-day Iraq, developed one of the earliest writing systems. They pressed damp clay into flat tablets and used a sharpened reed to make wedge-shaped impressions, a script now called cuneiform. At first, it was used to record how much grain, livestock, and trade goods people owned. Trained scribes spent years memorizing hundreds of different symbols. As a result, only a small portion of the population could read.

In ancient Egypt, scribes wrote with picture signs called hieroglyphs, often on papyrus, a paper-like material made from a tall reed that flourished along the Nile River.

About 3,000 years ago, Mediterranean traders known as the Phoenicians used an alphabet, a small set of letters that represent individual sounds. Because an alphabet was far easier to learn than hundreds of symbols, it spread quickly from place to place and gave rise to many later alphabets. The Arabic script, for example, developed from the writing of the Nabataeans, whose carved inscriptions can still be seen at Hegra, near AlUla in Saudi Arabia.

Paper was invented in China about 1,900 years ago. By around the year 800, Baghdad had established paper mills, and handwritten books, called manuscripts, multiplied throughout the Islamic world and beyond.

Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg of Germany built a printing press that used movable metal type, individual letters that could be rearranged and reused. Chinese printers had experimented with movable type centuries earlier, but Gutenberg's press made books dramatically faster and cheaper to produce in Europe, which helped literacy expand.

The typewriter appeared in the 1870s, and its keyboard layout is still used today. Now, with computers and smartphones, we can share our writing across the globe almost instantly. Yet each of these tools, from the reed to the keyboard, has served the same basic purpose: to help people hold on to their ideas and pass them to others who were not there to hear them.

versions.title: Writing Through Time: From Clay Tablets to Keyboards
versions.text:
Prior to the advent of writing, every civilization depended entirely and exclusively upon human memory for the preservation of knowledge. Stories, legal codes, and family histories were transmitted orally from one generation to the subsequent one through spoken language alone, and whenever an individual forgot some crucial detail, that irreplaceable knowledge could consequently vanish permanently and irretrievably. Writing fundamentally transformed this precarious situation, since it permitted words to endure considerably longer than any transient human voice and to travel far beyond the immediate location where they were originally spoken.

Approximately 5,000 years ago, the Sumerians of Mesopotamia, within present-day Iraq, developed one of humanity's earliest documented writing systems. They systematically pressed dampened clay into flat tablets and employed a sharpened reed implement to create characteristic wedge-shaped impressions, a distinctive script now historically designated cuneiform. Originally, this writing system served principally to document quantities of grain, livestock, and various commercial goods. Specially trained scribes consequently devoted many years to memorizing hundreds of distinct symbols, meaning only a comparatively small proportion of the broader population achieved genuine literacy.

Within ancient Egypt, professional scribes wrote using pictorial signs termed hieroglyphs, frequently inscribed upon papyrus, a paper-like material manufactured from a tall reed that flourished abundantly along the Nile River's fertile banks.

Approximately 3,000 years ago, Mediterranean merchants known as the Phoenicians developed an alphabet, a remarkably compact set of letters representing individual phonetic sounds rather than entire concepts. Because an alphabet proved considerably easier to master than memorizing hundreds of distinct symbols, it consequently spread rapidly across the ancient world and ultimately gave rise to numerous subsequent alphabetic systems. The Arabic script, for instance, developed directly from the writing system of the Nabataeans, whose carved inscriptions remain visible today at Hegra, near AlUla within Saudi Arabia.

Paper was invented within China approximately 1,900 years ago. By approximately the year 800, Baghdad had established dedicated paper mills, and handwritten books, termed manuscripts, consequently proliferated throughout the Islamic world and considerably beyond its borders, filling extensive libraries with scientific, mathematical, and literary works of considerable sophistication.

Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg of Germany constructed a sophisticated printing press employing movable metal type, individual letter forms that could be rearranged and reused indefinitely across countless printings. Chinese printers had experimented with movable type centuries earlier, yet Gutenberg's innovative press rendered books dramatically faster and considerably less expensive to produce throughout Europe specifically, which substantially contributed to a considerable expansion of widespread literacy.

The typewriter emerged during the 1870s, and its characteristic keyboard arrangement remains in continuous use today. Now, utilizing computers and smartphones, we can distribute our written communications across the entire globe almost instantaneously. Nevertheless, each of these successive technologies, extending from the humble reed to the modern keyboard, has consistently served an identical fundamental purpose: enabling people to preserve their ideas and transmit them to others who were not physically present to hear them originally spoken.

versions.title: Writing Through Time: From Clay Tablets to Keyboards
versions.text:
Prior to the historical advent of writing, every human civilization depended entirely and exclusively upon fallible human memory for the preservation of accumulated knowledge across successive generations. Stories, legal codes, and family histories were transmitted orally from one generation to the subsequent one exclusively through spoken language, and whenever an individual inevitably forgot some crucial detail, that irreplaceable knowledge could consequently vanish permanently and entirely irretrievably from collective memory. Writing fundamentally and irreversibly transformed this inherently precarious situation, since it permitted words to endure considerably longer than any transient human voice and to travel far beyond the immediate geographic location where they were originally spoken.

Approximately 5,000 years ago, the Sumerians of ancient Mesopotamia, within present-day Iraq, developed one of humanity's earliest documented and archaeologically verified writing systems. They systematically pressed dampened clay into flat rectangular tablets and employed a sharpened reed implement to create characteristic wedge-shaped impressions upon the soft surface, a distinctive script now historically designated cuneiform. Originally, this pioneering writing system served principally administrative functions, documenting quantities of grain, livestock, and various commercial goods for taxation and trade purposes. Specially trained scribes consequently devoted many years of their lives to memorizing hundreds of distinct cuneiform symbols, meaning only a comparatively small, specialized proportion of the broader population ever achieved genuine functional literacy.

Within ancient Egyptian civilization, professional scribes wrote using elaborate pictorial signs termed hieroglyphs, frequently inscribed upon papyrus, a specialized paper-like material manufactured laboriously from a tall reed species that flourished abundantly along the fertile banks of the Nile River.

Approximately 3,000 years ago, Mediterranean seafaring merchants known as the Phoenicians developed an alphabet, a remarkably compact, efficient set of letters representing individual phonetic sounds rather than entire conceptual ideas or objects. Because an alphabetic system proved considerably easier to master than memorizing hundreds of distinct symbolic characters, it consequently spread rapidly across the ancient Mediterranean world and ultimately gave rise to numerous subsequent alphabetic writing systems globally. The Arabic script, for instance, developed directly and historically from the writing system of the Nabataeans, whose elaborately carved inscriptions remain visible and legible today at Hegra, near AlUla within contemporary Saudi Arabia.

Paper was first invented within China approximately 1,900 years ago, representing a transformative manufacturing innovation. By approximately the year 800 of the common era, the city of Baghdad had established substantial dedicated paper mills, and handwritten books, termed manuscripts, consequently proliferated extensively throughout the broader Islamic world and considerably beyond its geographic borders, filling extensive scholarly libraries with scientific, mathematical, philosophical, and literary works of considerable intellectual sophistication.

Around the year 1450, Johannes Gutenberg of Germany constructed a sophisticated mechanical printing press employing movable metal type, individual letter forms cast in metal that could be systematically rearranged and reused indefinitely across countless successive printings. Chinese printers had experimented independently with movable type technology many centuries earlier, yet Gutenberg's innovative mechanical press rendered books dramatically faster to produce and considerably less expensive throughout Europe specifically, which substantially and measurably contributed to an extraordinary expansion of widespread popular literacy across the continent.

The mechanical typewriter emerged during the 1870s as a further technological innovation, and its characteristic keyboard arrangement remains in continuous, widespread use even today. Now, utilizing computers and smartphones, we can distribute our written communications across the entire globe almost instantaneously, communicating effortlessly with readers we will quite possibly never personally meet. Nevertheless, each of these successive historical technologies, extending continuously from the humble reed stylus to the modern digital keyboard, has consistently served an identical fundamental human purpose across millennia: enabling people to preserve their ideas durably and transmit them reliably to others who were not physically present to hear them originally spoken, sometimes across thousands of intervening years.

keyWords.definition: a person whose job was to write or copy things by hand, especially long ago
keyWords.example: The king asked a scribe to write down the new law.

keyWords.definition: a paper-like material made long ago from a tall water plant
keyWords.example: The old scroll was made of papyrus and was very fragile.

keyWords.definition: something new that someone creates for the first time
keyWords.example: The washing machine was an invention that saved people many hours.

keyWords.definition: to write down or save information so it can be used later
keyWords.example: Our class will record the temperature every morning.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Writing tools changed many times, helping words last and spread.
Only the Sumerians knew how to write.
The typewriter was the most important invention ever.
Paper is stronger and lasts longer than clay.
questions.why: The article follows writing from clay tablets to keyboards and shows how each step helped people save and share words.

wrong.B: The article also describes writing in Egypt, Phoenicia, China, and more.
wrong.C: The typewriter is one step, and the article does not rank it first.
wrong.D: The article does not compare the strength of paper and clay.

questions.stem: What were the first cuneiform marks mainly used for?
options: Writing long poems about brave kings
Printing books for schools
Keeping records of grain and trade
Sending letters to Egypt
questions.why: The article says cuneiform was first used to keep records of grain, animals, and trade.

wrong.A: The article does not say the first marks were poems.
wrong.B: Printing came thousands of years later.
wrong.D: The article does not mention letters to Egypt.

questions.stem: Who built a printing press with metal letters around 1450?
options: The Phoenicians
The Sumerians
A scribe in Baghdad
Johannes Gutenberg
questions.why: The article says Johannes Gutenberg of Germany built the printing press around 1450.

wrong.A: The Phoenicians used an early alphabet.
wrong.C: Baghdad is known in the article for its paper mills.

questions.stem: The article says cuneiform means "wedge-shaped." What does this tell you about the marks?
options: They were drawn in bright colors.
They were shaped like triangles or wedges.
They were round and smooth like circles.
They were tiny pictures of animals.
questions.why: A wedge is a shape that is thick at one end and pointed at the other, like the marks a reed made in clay.

wrong.A: The marks were pressed into clay, not colored.

questions.stem: Why did the alphabet spread quickly from place to place?
options: It was far easier to learn than many signs.
It could only be written on papyrus.
Kings ordered everyone to use it.
It was invented by Gutenberg in Germany.
questions.why: The article says an alphabet was far easier to learn than hundreds of symbols, so it spread quickly.

wrong.B: The article does not limit alphabets to papyrus.
wrong.C: The article does not mention kings ordering this.
wrong.D: Gutenberg lived thousands of years after the Phoenicians.

questions.stem: Why do you think only trained scribes could read and write in Sumer?
options: Clay was too expensive for others.
Writing was against the law.
Learning so many symbols took years.
Only scribes knew where to find reeds.
questions.why: The article says scribes spent years learning hundreds of symbols. Most people did not have that much time to study.

wrong.A: The article does not say clay was expensive.
wrong.B: The article does not say writing was illegal.
wrong.D: Reeds grew naturally, so they were easy to find.

questions.stem: What can you infer about books before the printing press?
options: They were cheap and easy for anyone to find.
They were made slowly by hand.
They were all written on clay.
They were typed on typewriters.
questions.why: The article says the press made books faster and cheaper, which suggests that earlier books took a long time to make and cost more.

wrong.A: The press made books cheaper, so they were costly before.
wrong.C: By then, paper was widely used.
wrong.D: Typewriters came in the 1870s, after the printing press.

questions.stem: How does the author mainly organize the article?
options: By comparing the problems and solutions of each country
By describing how to make each writing tool
By listing writing systems from easiest to hardest
In time order, from the earliest writing to today
questions.why: The article moves forward in time: cuneiform about 5,000 years ago, the alphabet about 3,000 years ago, paper, the printing press around 1450, the typewriter in the 1870s, and computers today.

wrong.A: The article does not organize ideas as problems and solutions by country.
wrong.B: The article does not give instructions for making tools.
wrong.C: The systems are ordered by date, not difficulty.

MID.prompt: Which change in writing do you think helped people the most? Explain your choice with details from the article.
checklist: I chose one change and named it clearly.
I gave at least two details from the article.
I explained how it helped people.
MID.modelAnswer: I think the alphabet helped people the most. The article says the Phoenicians used an alphabet with a small set of letters, which was much easier to learn than the hundreds of symbols a scribe had to study to read cuneiform. Because it was so much simpler, the alphabet spread quickly, and many later alphabets, such as Arabic and English, grew from it. This invention let far more people learn to read and record their own ideas instead of always needing a trained scribe.

keyWords.definition: a large, organized society with cities, laws, and its own culture
keyWords.example: The ancient Egyptian civilization built huge pyramids.

keyWords.definition: a book or document written by hand
keyWords.example: The library keeps an old manuscript in a glass case.

keyWords.definition: able to be moved or rearranged
keyWords.example: The classroom has movable desks for group work.

keyWords.definition: the ability to read and write
keyWords.example: The program helps adults improve their literacy.
New trees and benches will transform the empty lot into a park.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Each new tool helped people preserve and share ideas.
Cuneiform remains the best writing system.
Computers have replaced the need for anyone to read.
The Phoenicians invented paper and printing.
questions.why: The article traces writing from clay to keyboards and concludes that each tool served the purpose of preserving and passing on ideas.

wrong.B: The article describes cuneiform as an early system, not the best.
wrong.C: The article never makes this claim.
wrong.D: Paper came from China and printing from Gutenberg and earlier Chinese printers.

questions.stem: According to the article, the Arabic script developed from the writing of which people?
options: The Sumerians
The Egyptians
The Nabataeans
The Chinese
questions.why: The article says the Arabic script developed from the writing of the Nabataeans, whose inscriptions can be seen at Hegra near AlUla.

wrong.D: The article connects China with paper and early movable type.

questions.stem: What does the article say about movable type in China?
options: China never used any kind of printing.
Printers there tried it centuries before Gutenberg.
It was invented by the Sumerians in Mesopotamia.
It was only used for typewriters.
questions.why: The article states that Chinese printers had experimented with movable type centuries earlier.

wrong.A: The article says Chinese printers used movable type.
wrong.C: The Sumerians pressed marks into clay; they did not use movable type.

questions.stem: In the article, writing "transformed this situation." What does transformed mean?
options: Slowly forgot
Copied by hand
Completely changed
Kept the same
questions.why: Writing completely changed a world where knowledge depended only on memory.

wrong.A: Writing helped people remember, not forget.
wrong.B: Copying by hand is how manuscripts were made, not the meaning here.
wrong.D: Transformed means the opposite of staying the same.

questions.stem: How did Gutenberg's press affect literacy in Europe?
options: It reduced literacy because books became rare.
It had no effect at all on reading.
It ended the use of paper in Europe.
Cheaper books helped more people learn to read.
questions.why: The article says the press made books faster and less expensive to produce, which helped literacy expand.

wrong.A: Books became more common, not rare.
wrong.C: Printing used paper rather than ending it.

questions.stem: What can you infer about literacy in early Sumer compared with today?
options: Far fewer people could read then.
More people could read then than now.
Everyone could read cuneiform easily.
Only young children were allowed to learn to read.
questions.why: The article says only a small portion of the population could read because scribes had to memorize hundreds of symbols, unlike today's alphabets and widespread schooling.

wrong.D: The article does not say this.

questions.stem: Why might handwritten manuscripts have multiplied after Baghdad built paper mills?
options: Paper mills printed all of the books automatically.
Paper made the reeds grow faster.
Paper was cheaper and easier to make, so more copies were possible.
Clay tablets were banned.
questions.why: Since the article links paper mills to the growth of manuscripts and libraries, a ready supply of paper likely made copying books easier.

wrong.A: Manuscripts were handwritten, not printed by mills.
wrong.B: Paper has no effect on how plants grow.
wrong.D: The article does not say clay was banned.

questions.stem: Why does the author end with the idea that every tool, from the reed to the keyboard, served the same purpose?
options: To argue that keyboards should be replaced by reeds
To link thousands of years of change to one human need
To list the steps for making a reed pen at home
To show that writing has not changed at all
questions.why: The ending ties the whole history together by showing that every new tool met the same need to preserve and share ideas.

wrong.A: The author does not suggest returning to reeds.
wrong.C: The ending does not give instructions.
wrong.D: The article shows many changes; the purpose stayed the same.

HIGH.prompt: Choose two turning points in the history of writing. Explain how each one changed who could read and write, using evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained two turning points accurately.
I described how each affected literacy.
I supported my ideas with precise evidence.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Two major turning points in the history of writing were the invention of the alphabet and Gutenberg's printing press. The alphabet, used by the Phoenicians about 3,000 years ago, replaced hundreds of complicated symbols with a small set of letters, so ordinary people no longer needed years of training as a scribe to become literate. Centuries later, Gutenberg's press used movable metal letters to print books quickly and cheaply, which let more families than ever own a manuscript of their own instead of relying on handwritten copies. Together, these two changes transformed literacy from a skill reserved for royalty and scribes into something available to many more people.
